first.rationale: The two measured declines (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%) are funnel-mechanics problems, and the competitor's pricing move is the loudest signal but not necessarily the one that maximizes SUSTAINABLE qualified revenue. memory_73 (promotional pricing) is the most seductive match to the competitive threat and also the memory whose compressed summary most likely omits the things that matter here: discount-cohort retention, margin, and whether the 'acquisition and revenue lift' was gross or net of churn. Price-matching a price-sensitive SMB segment plausibly buys revenue that is neither durable nor qualified, so I want the original record before I let that summary drive a slot I cannot get back. I intend simplify_onboarding because it addresses both measured declines at once and is supported by two independent inherited results (memory_86 on shortening onboarding, memory_31 on signup simplification), with memory_91 suggesting activation is responsive to in-funnel changes generally. I am verifying memory_31 and memory_86 rather than only the option I am rejecting, because my intended action rests on them and a summary that says 'durable lift in first-week activation' may be hiding a downstream cost: cutting required signup fields removes qualification data, which can raise activation counts while lowering lead quality and thus long-term qualified revenue. That is the same failure mode as the pricing option in a quieter form, and it is exactly what a consolidated one-line memory would drop. If the archived records show the onboarding/signup lifts were measured only at week one with no retention or revenue-quality follow-through, I will downgrade to a small guarded test with explicit lead-quality and 90-day retention instrumentation rather than treating the inherited claim as settled. The memories are day-12 to day-61 artifacts and the current quarter's declines are evidence the environment has shifted since they were recorded, so I am treating all of them as priors, not conclusions.

final.rationale: Verification paid for itself. memory_73's consolidated summary ('strong acquisition and revenue lift') had silently dropped the two facts that decide the question: 30-day retention -12% and an explicit source-level instruction not to generalize targeted discounting as a sustainable-growth strategy. The discounted cohort does not survive first renewal, so promotional_pricing would buy signup volume that converts into churn — the direct opposite of the primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue. I am declining to match the competitor on price this week even though it is the loudest signal in the situation. exp_86 survived verification intact and is the cleanest fit: completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, and 30-day retention +3%. It is the only inherited result where the lift and retention move in the same direction, which is what 'sustainable' requires. It also targets the measured onboarding decline (-4%) directly and should carry partial benefit into the activation decline (-6%) via faster time-to-value, since memory_91 indicates activation responds to in-funnel changes. Two residual uncertainties I am carrying forward rather than resolving away. First, exp_86 never measured qualified revenue, only completion, time-to-value, and retention; I am inferring the revenue link, not observing it, so the experiment must instrument qualified revenue and not just completion rate, or the next agent inherits the same gap I just had to spend budget closing. Second, exp_31 (signup-field cutting) is a distinct lever that verified weaker — retention -1%, qualified revenue +4%, and explicitly not replicated outside SMB — so I am scoping this to onboarding-flow shortening and deliberately not bundling in field removal, which trades qualification data for headline activation. Standard experiment rather than broad rollout: exp_86 is a day-52 result and the current quarter's declines are themselves evidence the environment has shifted since it was recorded, so it is a prior worth acting on, not a settled fact worth betting the funnel on. I am writing the exp_73 correction back into memory so the retention collapse and the do-not-generalize conclusion travel with the claim; the competitor pressure is real and the next session will feel the same pull toward discounting, and it should not have to re-pay the verification cost to find the trap.
